source: MAFF / Boosting Food Production Program (PMO), Royal Government of Cambodia — ខ្សែសង្វាក់ផលិតកម្ម ដំណាំស្វាយចន្ទីនៅកម្ពុជា (Cashew Value Chain Study in Cambodia), field survey report (250 household respondents across major cashew-growing provinces), 2017, 57pp
text:
Identification and impact of a newly-emerging cashew pest that surveyed farmers referred to as 'mousetè' (មូសតែ, literally 'tea mosquito'), from the 2017 MAFF cashew value chain study.

At the time of the study, farmers reported that over the preceding roughly two years they had faced increasing damage from this pest, but had no research documentation or formal identification available to them for it.

The study's own photographic documentation identifies the insect as a tea mosquito bug in the genus Helopeltis, showing what appear to be three related forms/species: Helopeltis bradyi, Helopeltis antonii, and Helopeltis theivora. This genus is a well-known pest of both tea and cashew crops in the region, and the report notes it has also been observed in other cashew- and tea-growing countries such as Vietnam.

Damage pattern: the pest attacks young flush leaves and shoots first, causing wilting and curling, then spreads to other leaves and tender growth, producing necrotic brown spotting; in severe infestations this leads to significant defoliation of the tree canopy. When it attacks flowers, it reduces flower and subsequent fruit set, directly cutting that season's yield.

Farmers reported the pest appears more during hot, dry, and windy periods but said they did not have clear knowledge of its full life cycle or a reliably effective control method — repeated pesticide spraying was used, but often did not fully control it, and treatment cost was reported at around 100,000 riel per spray application, with some farmers spending roughly 1 million riel per hectare per year and still not achieving good control.

This pest problem was reported as a serious enough concern that, at the time of the survey, about 4% of farmers said they intended to abandon cashew growing entirely because of it, and about 10% said they were considering reducing their cashew-planted area over the following 1-5 years. The report's authors explicitly recommend urgent research to properly document this pest's biology and develop an effective, farmer-accessible control recommendation.
caveat: Some specific figures in this source (percentages, price points, yield ranges) were transcribed from a scanned document at a resolution where certain digits were hard to confirm with full pixel-level certainty. Figures are reported as best-effort readings of the source; anyone using exact numbers for decisions should verify against the original report where possible.
